\section[\texorpdfstring{\fa{نوه} (nave)}{نوه (nave)}]{\fa{نوه} (nave) — a grandchild}

\label{lesson:FA-C117-nave}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Persian for a baker, then the Persian for a small child.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \fa{نوه}}
\textbf{\fa{نوه}} — \emph{nave} — \textquotedblleft{}a grandchild\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{nave} is usually traced to the old Iranian word for \textquotedblleft{}grandson\textquotedblright{} that Old Persian wrote \emph{napā}, the same Indo-European word as Latin \emph{nepos}, \textquotedblleft{}grandson\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for this chapter.
\end{grammarlens}

  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{nave}, once more

  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Persian for a baker, then the Persian for a small child, then say \emph{nave} again
\end{itemize}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\fa{هواپیما} (havâpeymâ)}{هواپیما (havâpeymâ)}]{\fa{هواپیما} (havâpeymâ) — an aeroplane}

\label{lesson:FA-C117-havapeyma}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Persian for the metro, then the Persian for a ship.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \fa{هواپیما}}
\textbf{\fa{هواپیما}} — \emph{havâpeymâ} — \textquotedblleft{}an aeroplane\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{havâpeymâ} is \emph{havâ}, \textquotedblleft{}air\textquotedblright{}, with \emph{-peymâ}, \textquotedblleft{}measuring, crossing\textquotedblright{} (from \emph{peymudan}): the air-crosser. \emph{havâ} is borrowed from Arabic \emph{hawāʾ}, \textquotedblleft{}air\textquotedblright{} (root \emph{h-w-y}, Lane); \emph{peymâ} is native Persian.
\end{cousinweb}
